lines.text: אין 44 איש
אַיִן, but intensive, none, not one; see on
this idiom in מִן 1. b. ב. Jer. 10, 6. 7. 30,
7. So מֵאֵין יוֹשֵׁב i. q. אֵין יוֹשֵׁב, Is. 5, 9.
Note. The absol. form אַיִן stands
only at the end of a clause; while
the constr. אֵין everywhere depends on
something following; e. g. Num. 20, 5
מַיִם אַיִן there is no water, for which
might also be said אֵין מַיִם.
II. אַיִן adv. of interrog. where? Arab.
أَيْنَ; found only with מִן prefixed, מֵאַיִן
whence? Gen. 29, 4. Nah. 3, 7. al.—Ori-
ginally this was the same with the
negat. אַיִן I, and passed over into the
interrogative sense; hence by apoc. אַי,
אֵי, אִי III. See in אַי no. 1. Heb.
Gram. § 150. 1. fin.
אִין 1 Sam. 21, 9, i. q. אַיִן, but inter-
rogatively for הֲאֵין.
אִיעֶזֶר see אֲבִיעֶזֶר.
אֵיפָה, rarely אֵפָה, f. an ephah, a
measure of grain, containing three seahs,
סְאָה, or ten omers, עֹמֶר, Ex. 16, 36.
According to Josephus, Ant. 8. 2. 9, the
ephah contained 72 sextarii, equal to the
Attic (liquid) metretes, or 1993.95 Paris
cubic inches, about 1 ⅑ bush. English;
see Boeckh Metrolog. Untersuch. pp.
259, 278. This is also confirmed by
other testimony; so that there is doubt-
less an error in another passage of Jose-
phus, Ant. 15. 9. 2, where the ephah
seems to be equal to 96 sextarii, or the
Attic medimnus. 1 Sam. 17, 17. Zech.
5, 6 sq. Judg. 6, 19. Ruth 2, 17. Also
אֵיפָה וְאֵיפָה a double ephah, one just,
the other false, Prov. 20, 10. Deut. 25,
14. Am. 8, 5.—The origin of this word
is to be sought in the Egyptian lan-
guage; where the Heb. אֵיפָה corre-
sponds to ⲱⲓⲡⲓ measure, spec. of corn,
modius, from r. ⲱⲡ, ⲏⲡ, to number;
whence Sept. οἰφί, Arab. ويبة, an Egyp-
tian measure. See Rödiger in Allg.
Encyclop. art. Epha. Thes. Ling. Heb.
in Append.
אֵיפֹה (from אֵי and פֹּה here) where?
Is. 49, 21. Ruth 2, 19; how? what kind
of? Judg. 8, 18. In an indirect inquiry,
אֵיפוֹא i. q. אֵפוֹא, q. v.
* אִישׁ, c. suff. אִישִׁי, אִישֵׁךְ, אִישָׁהּ;
Plur. אִישִׁים only thrice, Ps. 141, 4. Prov.
8, 4. Is. 53, 3; instead of which the com-
mon usage has substituted אֲנָשִׁים (from
obsol. sing. אֱנָשׁ), constr. אַנְשֵׁי, c. suff.
אֲנָשָׁיו, אַנְשֵׁיהֶם; also as periphrastic plur.
בְּנֵי אִישׁ, comp. no. 6.
1. a man. Spec. a) a male, opp. to
a female; Gen. 4, 1 I have gotten a man
with the Lord, i. e. a man-child. 1 Sam.
1, 11. So even of brutes, Gen. 7, 2;
comp. 1, 27. 6, 19. So Lat. vir of beasts,
Virg. Eclog. 7, 7. b) a husband, opp.
to a wife, Ruth 1, 11. Gen. 3, 6. 29, 32.
34. With suff. אֲנָשֵׁינוּ our men, i. e. our
husbands, Jer. 44, 19. So Gr ἀνήρ Il.
18. 291; Lat. vir Hor. Sat. 1. 2. 127. c)
As opp. to an old man, one of manly age,
vigour, 1 Sam. 2, 33. d) Emphat. of
manliness, warlike valour, comp. Hithpa.
below. 1 Sam. 4, 9 הִתְחַזְּקוּ וִהְיוּ לַאֲנָשִׁים
be strong, and be ye men! 1 K. 2, 2.
Comp. Hom. Il. 5. 529. e) a man, mor-
tal, opp. to God, Job 9, 32. 12, 10. Is. 31,
8; espec. in plur. Gen. 32, 29. Is. 7, 13.
Comp. Hom. πατὴρ ἀνδρῶν τε θεῶν τε.
Opp. to beasts, Ex. 11, 7. Gen. 49, 6.
f) Joined in apposition with other sub-
stantives, as אִישׁ סָרִיס a man a eunuch
i. e. a eunuch Jer. 38, 7; אִישׁ כֹּהֵן a
priest Lev. 21, 9; espec. with gentile
names, e. g. אִישׁ עִבְרִי a Hebrew Gen.
39, 14. Comp. Gr. ἄνδρες Γαλιλαῖοι, ἄν-
δρες Ἰσραηλῖται, Acts 1, 11. 3, 12. g)
With genit. of a city, land, people, it de-
notes a citizen, inhabitant, etc. e. g. אִישׁ
יִשְׂרָאֵל a man of Israel, i. e. Israelite;
אַנְשֵׁי יִשְׂרָאֵל 1 Sam. 7, 11; אַנְשֵׁי יְהוּדָה
2 Sam. 19, 42; also אַנְשֵׁי הָעִיר Gen. 24,
13. In this signif. the sing. אִישׁ is mostly
put collectively, as אִישׁ יִשְׂרָאֵל for אַנְשֵׁי
22. al. h) With genit. of a king, leader,
military chief, master, etc. the men of
any one, for his companions, followers,
soldiers, his people, 1 Sam. 23, 3. 12. 24,
5. 8. 28, 1. Once perhaps spoken of
relatives and near friends, like Syr.
ܐܢ̈ܫܳܐ ܕܝܠܗ, e. g. Ez. 24, 17. 22, where
לֶחֶם אֲנָשִׁים the bread of men, is the food
which relatives and friends were accus-
tomed to send to mourners. i) So too
אִישׁ אֱלֹהִים and with art, אִישׁ הָאֱלֹהִים,

line_status.note: The shin in the right‑hand header word איש is printed without a shin dot (header is unpointed); Reading B's שׁ adds a dot not on the page. Order and letters otherwise identical.
Printed order (right-to-left) is מַיִם then אַיִן (the pausal form from Num. 20:5, with patah under aleph and hiriq under yod), not אֵין מַיִם — that tsere form appears only on line 3.

The printed order is אֵין first (rightmost), then מַיִם, i.e. the construct form אֵין (tsere) placed before the noun — the point of the contrast with line 2's מַיִם אַיִן. Reading A inverts the order and gives patach instead of tsere.
The vowel under the final aleph on line 1 is a horizontal bar (patach), not two dots (tsere); the tsere form אֵי is the first item of line 2, so Reading B is correct.

First word has tsere (two dots) under aleph and no dagesh in the yod; the word after "See in" has patach (אַי), matching the אַי at the end of line 1 — Reading A's dagesh and tsere there are not printed.
Headword has a single hiriq dot under the aleph (אִין, as in B), but the second word is printed with patah under aleph and hiriq under yod (אַיִן, as in A) — each reading got one word right.

The Arabic word ends in tā' marbūṭa (ة, two dots clearly printed above the final round letter), not plain hā' (ه) as in A; and no fatḥa is printed over the initial wāw — the only marks are the consonant dots of ي, ب and ة. Reading B matches the print exactly.
Headword is plene אֵיפוֹא — a distinct vav stroke carries the ḥolem between פ and א (A right, B wrong); but the comma after אֵפוֹא is printed with a space before it (B right, A wrong).

Printed left-to-right order: אַנְשֵׁי יִשְׂרָאֵל stands at the left (line start), then "1 Sam. 7, 11 ;", then אַנְשֵׁי יְהוּדָה at the right edge (continuing to "2 Sam. 19, 42" on the next line). Reading A swaps the two phrases; Reading B matches. Pointing in both is otherwise identical and correct (shin dot in אַנְשֵׁי, sin dot in יִשְׂרָאֵל, shureq in יְהוּדָה).

The printed Syriac is two words, ܐܢܫܐ (right, with seyame) followed by ܕܝܠܗ (left) — "his men/relatives", not ܠܚܡܐ ܕܐܢܫܐ; no initial lamadh‑ḥeth‑mim word is printed. Reading A has the correct words; Reading B invented the "bread of men" phrase (that is the Hebrew on line 2). Pointing on the right word is sparse (seyame plus a zqapha-like mark); other small marks are too faint to read with confidence.
